The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an update in 2001 regarding fatal and severe liver injuries associated with the use of rifampin and pyrazinamide for the treatment of latent tuberculosis infection. This update also included revisions to the recommendations provided by the American Thoracic Society and the CDC. The findings were published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), highlighting the need for careful monitoring of liver function during such treatments. [Reference: MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly. 2001;50:733–5. DOI: https://pubmed.gov/11787580] 2. Voogt GR and Schoeman HS explored the ototoxicity of aminoglycoside drugs used in tuberculosis treatment. Their 1996 study, published in the South African Journal of Communication Disorders, emphasized the potential for hearing loss and other auditory complications in patients receiving these medications. [Reference: S Afr J Commun Disord. 1996;43:3–6. PMID: 9265840] 3. Gülbay BE and colleagues conducted a study on the side effects caused by primary antituberculosis drugs during the initial phase of therapy in 1,149 hospitalized tuberculosis patients. Published in Respiratory Medicine in 2006, the study detailed the frequency and types of adverse events, underscoring the importance of monitoring and managing these effects to ensure treatment adherence and success. [Reference: Respir Med. 2006;100:1834–42.] 4. Bloss E and collaborators investigated adverse events related to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) treatment in Latvia between 2000 and 2004. Their findings, published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2010, highlighted the challenges of managing side effects in MDR-TB patients and the need for improved treatment protocols. [Reference: Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2010;14:275–81. PMID: 20132617] 5. Oxlade O, Falzon D, and Menzies D evaluated the impact and cost-effectiveness of strategies to detect drug-resistant tuberculosis. Their 2012 study, published in the European Respiratory Journal, provided evidence supporting the implementation of diagnostic tools to improve treatment outcomes and reduce transmission. [Reference: Eur Respir J. 2012;39:626–34.] 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) released consolidated guidelines in 2016 on the detection of katG and inhA mutations to guide the use of isoniazid and ethionamide in drug-resistant tuberculosis. These guidelines emphasized the importance of molecular diagnostics in tailoring treatment regimens for patients with resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. [Reference: Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2016;20:1099–104.] 7. The WHO's 2022 update to its consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment included recommendations for managing drug-resistant tuberculosis. These updates incorporated new evidence and recommendations, such as the use of bedaquiline and delamanid in children under six years of age and the introduction of shorter, all-oral regimens for eligible patients. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of individualized treatment plans based on drug susceptibility testing. [Reference: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Module 4, 2022 Update.] 8. Blumberg HM and colleagues published clinical practice guidelines in 2003 for the treatment of tuberculosis, developed by the American Thoracic Society, CDC, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. These guidelines provided comprehensive recommendations for the management of tuberculosis, including drug-susceptible and drug-resistant cases. [Reference: Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2003;167:603–62.] 9. Ahmad Khan F and collaborators conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2012 on the treatment of active tuberculosis in patients with HIV infection. Their findings, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, highlighted the complexities of co-managing tuberculosis and HIV, emphasizing the need for integrated care approaches. [Reference: Clin Infect Dis. 2012;55:1154–63.] 10. The WHO's 2010 revision of its guidelines on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection in adults and adolescents provided a public health approach to managing co-infections, including tuberculosis. These guidelines emphasized the timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation during tuberculosis treatment to optimize outcomes. [Reference: WHO Guidelines, 2010 Revision.] 11. Abdool Karim SS and colleagues published a landmark study in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2010, demonstrating that early initiation of antiretroviral therapy during tuberculosis treatment significantly improved survival rates in co-infected patients. This study provided critical evidence for integrating HIV and tuberculosis care. [Reference: N Engl J Med. 2010;362:697–706.] 12. Friedrich SO and collaborators assessed the sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay as an early sputum biomarker for tuberculosis treatment response. Their 2013 study, published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine, highlighted the assay's potential to guide treatment decisions and monitor patient progress. [Reference: Lancet Respir Med. 2013;1:462–70.] 13. The WHO's 2022 update to its guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment included recommendations for the use of bedaquiline in longer regimens for patients aged six years and older. These guidelines emphasized the importance of including effective agents in treatment regimens to improve outcomes and reduce the risk of resistance development. [Reference: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Module 4, 2022 Update.] 14. Surgery has been explored as an adjunctive treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Fox GJ and colleagues conducted a meta-analysis in 2016, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, which demonstrated that surgical interventions could improve treatment outcomes in select patients. [Reference: Clin Infect Dis. 2016;62:887–95.] 15. The WHO's 2022 guidelines on tuberculosis treatment emphasized the use of shorter, all-oral regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis patients who meet specific eligibility criteria. These regimens aim to improve adherence, reduce treatment duration, and minimize adverse events. [Reference: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Module 4, 2022 Update.
